title: Warnings About Appetite, Money and Wine
overview: A teacher, speaking like a parent, warns a young person about the hidden traps in food, wealth, flattery, sex and drink, and urges them to value wisdom and honor their parents.

parts.label: Dining with the powerful (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: "Put a knife to your throat" is a vivid way of saying: hold your appetite firmly in check at a ruler's table. The rich food is called deceptive, probably because it tastes good but does you harm, or because a powerful host's generosity may come with strings attached.

parts.label: Riches with wings (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Do not wear yourself out chasing wealth or trust your own clever schemes to get it. Money can vanish as suddenly as an eagle taking off, gone before you can stop it.

parts.label: False welcomes and stolen land (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: A stingy host who says "eat and drink" while counting every bite spoils the meal, and good advice is wasted on someone set on mocking it. Moving a boundary stone, the marker of a family's inherited land, was a quiet way to rob orphans, but the text warns that God acts as their Defender, like a strong relative who takes up their case.

parts.label: Correction and a parent's joy (vv. 12-18)
parts.note: The lines about the rod reflect the physical punishment that was normal in that culture, and their point is that correcting a child steers them away from a life that ends in ruin; readers today differ on how to apply them. The teacher also says not to envy people who do well by doing wrong, because a lasting future belongs to those who honor God.

parts.label: Stay sober, honor your parents (vv. 19-25)
parts.note: Heavy drinkers and gluttons end up sleepy, broke and in rags. Listening to your father, not looking down on your mother when she is old, and holding on to truth like something you would never sell are what make a family glad.

parts.label: Two deep traps (vv. 26-35)
parts.note: An affair is pictured as a deep, narrow pit that is hard to climb out of, set by someone who waits like a bandit. Then comes a sharp, almost comic portrait of a drunk: the wine sparkles but bites like a snake, leaving you seeing strange things, swaying as if asleep on a ship's mast, beaten without feeling it, and already wanting another drink.

think: Which of the pulls described here, whether appetite, money, flattery or drink, have you seen take hold of someone before they noticed it happening?
